scope: One Garden Adventure demo; audit existing agreements, current implementation, and September 14 user corrections. No new gameplay design selected.
coreInstruction: Read and discuss, choose and confirm in the reading/conversation area. The action and consequences happen in the game world.
latestSteering: Finish the inventory of what is wrong and missing before making further decisions. The proposed flashback is not approved.
checkboxMeaning: Accepted connected feature, not prose or a partial handler. All checkboxes remain open; PRESENT identifies existing functionality without pretending it is missing.

groups.title: Purpose, opening, and the whole journey

items.title: An independently understandable adventure
items.current: Tony cannot explain the current journey from A to Z after playing it. Passing handler tests did not establish this.
items.acceptance: A fresh player can explain who they are helping, what the current problem is, what they can do, and what changed, using the game itself.

items.title: Jo, Loop, and the entry into Pip's world
items.current: Jo and Loop are modeled and the introduction exists. Begin jumps to the river; the projection and return framing are weak.
items.acceptance: The ready studio clearly introduces Pip's story, the child's role, and the transition into the playable world without an equipment quest.

items.title: The seed promise and its stakes
items.current: The opening says plant with Grandma before dark. It is largely a text premise; its relationship to the larger story needs a visible payoff.
items.acceptance: The seed, Grandma, planting place, promise, and later story memory remain connected throughout play.

items.title: Why the garden became quiet
items.current: The letter, Mara's explanation, and Sol's doubt exist in separate panels. Their relationship is not established as a coherent investigation.
items.acceptance: The child encounters Grandma's belief, each actual reason, and the changed understanding through connected scenes.

items.title: Storm chronology
items.current: Correct past facts exist in prose, but the broken crossing dominates the visible problem and can imply it caused all absence.
items.acceptance: Work changes and Sol's reluctance precede the storm; repairing the bridge visibly solves access without pretending it solves work or confidence.

items.title: One complete chapter and a separate recording
items.current: A route reaches an ending. Actual coherent pacing, independent enjoyment, and a final three-minute recording have not been accepted.
items.acceptance: The full bounded chapter works independently; recording length does not replace story completeness or introduce filler.

items.title: Child role versus Pip, storyteller, and narrator
items.current: Controls alternate among Pip movement, director construction, first-person Sol writing, and Loop narration with insufficient transition context.
items.acceptance: Every change of role identifies whose actions or words the child controls and returns to the correct game situation.

items.title: All gameplay resolves in the world
items.current: Confirmations often leave the player in a reader, planner, or miniature rehearsal rather than showing the action and consequence in the game.
items.acceptance: Apply Tony's latest instruction: read/speak/choose/confirm in the reading area, then perform and observe the action and consequence in the game world.

items.title: Purposeful tasks instead of following buttons
items.current: Most later progress consists of opening a panel and selecting a supplied successful continuation.
items.acceptance: The reading gives information needed to make a meaningful decision; the confirmed decision has an understandable world consequence and a reason for the next task.

items.title: Literal, age-appropriate language
items.current: Titles and full passages exist, but references such as finish the ending and what did the repair make possible are not grounded in the player's experience.
items.acceptance: Each instruction has a clear actor, object, action, and reason understandable to ages 9–12; challenging vocabulary receives support without vague prose.

items.title: Recognizable places with functions
items.current: Studio, dock, river, workshop, and garden exist; the workshop is a small outside façade and there is no bakery destination or playable bakery scene.
items.acceptance: Every required place has a clear purpose, approach, relevant objects, and observable activity. The bakery requirement stays open until its connection is resolved with Tony.

items.title: Distinguishable character identities
items.current: Named main characters exist. Reused Rina, boy, and Sol models also depict generic passengers or remembered people.
items.acceptance: The child can identify who is speaking or acting, and historical people or passengers cannot be mistaken for another active character.

items.title: Usable objects versus scenery
items.current: Broken scraps, ready-made bridge sections, tiny posts, seed boat, workshop props, and flowers have inconsistent cues and interactivity.
items.acceptance: A player can tell which objects are usable, why, and how; decorative objects do not appear to promise unavailable actions.

items.title: Where the planks came from
items.current: Two completed bridge decks begin on the bank. Nearby broken wood is decoration with no recovery, inspection, or collection action.
items.acceptance: Establish the source and intended use of the material in play; account for Tony's requested wood collection without silently inventing quantities or a crafting system.

items.title: Collecting and using materials
items.current: The state and commands have no wood/tool/material pickup, carry, use, or consumption sequence.
items.acceptance: The requested collection has a concrete world source, purpose, player action, item state, use, and consequence. Exact mechanics remain an audit follow-up, not an approved new design.

items.title: Backpack purpose
items.current: The backpack is a possession list for seed, letter, Mara's copy, and Grandma's return copy. It is not connected to material collection and its purpose is easy to miss.
items.acceptance: The player understands what is carried, where it came from, what it is for, and what changes when it is used or given away.

items.title: Backpack contents and ownership
items.current: Seed/page ownership changes are modeled and displayed. Sol keeps his manuscript; reading a page does not generally create possession.
items.acceptance: Verify contents against visible pickup, handoff, planting, return delivery, and restart; preserve the distinction between owned items and readable story records.

items.title: Using an item at the relevant place
items.current: Plant/share/give buttons select the item automatically; the item-to-task connection is mostly explanatory text.
items.acceptance: The game makes the actual item, recipient or target, and resulting transfer unmistakable. Manual inventory selection is not assumed to be the answer.

items.title: World scale and camera readability
items.current: In the audit view, the whole island shrinks while the construction panel scrolls; posts and damaged bridge details become hard to identify.
items.acceptance: Required objects, hands, materials, attachment points, and consequences remain readable at the demo viewport without exact-pixel searching.

groups.title: Mara, her work, and the passenger boat

items.title: Mara doing her job when first met
items.current: Mara stands at an empty dock. The passenger boat and passengers are hidden during planning.
items.acceptance: The game establishes her actual work and why she cannot leave, before asking the child to solve her scheduling problem.

items.title: Passenger boat distinct from seed boat
items.current: A separate passenger vessel is constructed, but it only appears for a later gathering and uses a scaled seed-boat model.
items.acceptance: The passenger vessel is recognizable in purpose, size, route, and timing and cannot be confused with seed transport or bridge material.

items.title: People affected by Mara's duty
items.current: Two passengers exist only during the final arrival animation and disappear ashore. There is no pre-decision evidence of the people she must help.
items.acceptance: The obligation to passengers is observable and relevant to the child's plan; passenger-management mechanics are not silently invented.

items.title: The time conflict before choosing
items.current: Usual time and after the last boat returns are text choices. The difference is not established through the working dock and gathering context.
items.acceptance: The child can explain what overlaps and what postponement changes without needing an external explanation or a forced real-time wait.

items.title: Bridge repair does not finish her work
items.current: The original bridge-only conversational misunderstanding is absent as a direct offer. A later optional explanation box is the remaining avenue.
items.acceptance: Preserve a meaningful way to discover the difference between access and availability, with a specific character response and world evidence.

items.title: An offer versus an agreed invitation
items.current: The first later-time offer is transient local reply state; actual invitations are saved separately, but the interface does not clearly distinguish the two.
items.acceptance: After each conversation the child knows what has been proposed, agreed, still needs telling, and will happen next.

items.title: Story copy and permission
items.current: Take-page ownership and animation exist, but the reader remains open and obscures the world handoff.
items.acceptance: Mara visibly gives permission and the actual copy, then the game shows Pip carrying it; this does not imply she is attending.

items.title: Reciprocity while Mara works
items.current: Copy delivery back to Mara is modeled at the end. The child's proposed answer is not used to form the commitment.
items.acceptance: Mara's wish to hear a story is connected to a comprehensible promise and actual later return delivery.

items.title: Consequences of all three arrangements
items.current: Usual/Pip, later/Pip, and later/Mara affect state, attendance, and ending wording; their preparation and payoff are largely panels.
items.acceptance: The selected time, work, travel, teller/listener roles, and return-copy duty are visible in the game world for each arrangement.

items.title: The original damage and the repair task
items.current: Broken scraps appear at a different crossing from the usable construction spot. There is little connection between that damage and the loose decks.
items.acceptance: The player understands what broke, what can be reused or repaired, and what the resulting route will connect.

items.title: Placement based on visible reach
items.current: reaches() requires the bridge center within 0.22 world units of z=3 or z=-2, in addition to visible bank overlap. This hidden rule rejects otherwise plausible positions.
items.acceptance: Visible geometry and feedback explain valid placement; no hidden exact-position requirement without an obvious corresponding world target.

items.title: Opposing posts and attachment targets
items.current: Four small posts exist. They sit at z+0.53 while validity tests the bridge center at z, and the valid pair is not explained.
items.acceptance: If a required location remains, opposing posts and the placement instruction unambiguously show it, as Tony requested.

items.title: Joining the sections
items.current: Joining requires near-exact spacing and alignment; only generic short-ends feedback is shown.
items.acceptance: Ordinary dragging or native controls make contact, orientation, preview, join, and failure readable without numerical knowledge.

items.title: Wide versus narrow river challenge
items.current: River width and fixed deck length exist, but a hidden coordinate stripe competes with the intended reach reasoning.
items.acceptance: The child can predict and observe a genuine reach difference, then move the same materials without rescaling them.

items.title: Fastening each real end
items.current: Two buttons and rope states exist; posts are tiny and some controls fall below the fold.
items.acceptance: Each end has an obvious loose/secure state and corresponding world fastening; one fastening does not imply both are secure.

items.title: Ordinary unsecured crossing attempt
items.current: Main Go to Grandma requires bridgeReady. Try crossing requires the hidden alignment rule; normal movement can emit the old loose-end block. Tony reports the requested attempt remains inaccessible.
items.acceptance: Keyboard movement, scene clicking, and named movement all let Pip step onto a reaching but unsecured bridge and trigger the consequence.

items.title: Collapse, retreat, and rebuilding
items.current: A three-second collapse handler and animation exist after bridgeAttemptable succeeds. This is not proof the player can trigger it through normal placement and movement.
items.acceptance: The bridge visibly fails, Pip returns safely, pieces have a readable new location, and rebuilding is required while unrelated progress survives.

items.title: Honest feedback for the actual failure
items.current: GO and blocked keyboard movement can report fastening when the real cause is placement or a gap.
items.acceptance: Gap, alignment, loose connection, obstruction, and unavailable action receive distinct relevant feedback.

items.title: Construction role and current instruction
items.current: The audit entered construction while the goal still said Talk to Mara; joining, fastening, and Back to Pip were below the initial visible panel.
items.acceptance: The active construction task, controls, current selection, confirmation, and return to Pip are clear at once without a competing instruction.

items.title: Seed-boat channel and permanent route
items.current: The placement code reserves a hidden channel; warnings refer to farther along the river. The completed bridge then locks in place.
items.acceptance: The navigable boat route and retained bridge are visually understandable; no invisible exclusion area or later disappearing route.

items.title: Recovery and successful alternatives
items.current: State preserves the five physical histories and collapses only the bridge arrangement. Existing tests use controlled placement.
items.acceptance: Exercise ordinary-input success with no mistake, one loose end, two loose ends, repeated recovery, seed-first, carried-seed, and save interruption.

items.title: A reason to send the seed first
items.current: Sending it ahead changes ownership, but Pip must still make the same crossing; the purpose or consequence of the alternative is weakly communicated.
items.acceptance: The child understands what sending ahead accomplishes, what it does not accomplish, and how it differs from carrying it.

items.title: Actual cargo movement and receipt
items.current: A separate seed boat moves with the seed and Grandma walks to receive it. This is one of the existing world actions.
items.acceptance: Ordinary play visibly preserves seed identity, cargo transfer, Pip on shore, and Grandma returning with it.

items.title: Boat limits and harmless later use
items.current: The note says the boat cannot carry Pip. Later Watch the empty seed boat is a bobbing action with little gameplay purpose.
items.acceptance: Boat actions and limits are intelligible; an empty demonstration is not counted as another substantive game mechanic.

items.title: Pip and Grandma plant together
items.current: Planting changes state and the seed moves, but the Grandma reader can remain open during the action.
items.acceptance: Confirmation returns attention to the game, shows both characters and the real seed being planted, and returns to the resulting situation.

items.title: Roots, soil, and the flower
items.current: Soil, growth, and bloom states exist; the seed does not bloom in the boat or hand.
items.acceptance: The visible growth follows actual planting, survives interruption once, and is clearly the fulfillment of the seed promise.

items.title: Planting changes the next objective
items.current: The goal changes to finding stories, but it immediately exposes several competing destinations and library actions.
items.acceptance: A visible response from Grandma connects keeping the promise to finding out why stories and visits stopped.

groups.title: First garden visit and lantern purpose

items.title: Grandma explains her garden
items.current: The agreed first-visit explanation about old stories and waiting lanterns is missing. A library button appears instead.
items.acceptance: Grandma establishes what the lanterns are, why they hold stories, and why new contributions matter before the library is used as a task.

items.title: Old stories versus current tasks
items.current: The Windy Picnic and The Unexpected Duet are available immediately after crossing. A short older-story label does not explain why the player is seeing them.
items.acceptance: Clearly identify these as earlier contributions, their owners, optional purpose, and how to return to the ongoing adventure.

items.title: Empty flowers waiting for stories
items.current: The three reserved NPC flowers are hidden until their records exist, rather than visible empty rooted lanterns waiting for contributions.
items.acceptance: The player can see and inspect old contributions, waiting places, and Pip's separately planted flower before the corresponding sharing events.

items.title: Selecting a particular world lantern
items.current: All flowers use the same lanterns target and open the same library grid; they do not open their own named story directly.
items.acceptance: Each world lantern identifies and opens its own page, author, status, and picture, with the current goal retained.

items.title: New story enters its lantern
items.current: Record flags show flowers or library cards. There is no staged Grandma exchange and visible title/picture transfer into the selected world flower.
items.acceptance: Sharing causes the visible world lantern to gain the correct title, author, page, and supported image once.

items.title: Grandma's belief changes through information
items.current: A saved report flag changes replies, but the report panel has two buttons that dispatch the same explanation and the world reaction is absent.
items.acceptance: The player sees what Pip communicated and how Grandma's understanding changes; no automatic claim that the child explained it.

items.title: Sol-first and Grandma-first continuity
items.current: State supports alternate visit orders. Several generic greetings and goals do not demonstrate the promised conditional conversational sequence.
items.acceptance: Each character responds only to what has been told, and a completed visit does not become a purposeless repeat errand.

items.title: Library purpose after the ending
items.current: Old and new pages remain available with separate authors and draft status. Their physical relationship to the garden is weak.
items.acceptance: Revisit the same world contributions without duplicates, reset, required rereading, or a claim that opening them proves comprehension.

items.title: Who is telling which event
items.current: The full page has author attribution, but the transition from current Mara to her remembered boy-and-bird account is not staged.
items.acceptance: Establish teller, setting, chronology, and the child's role before presenting the events or choices.

items.title: Boy, damaged wing, promise, and hesitation
items.current: These exist as sentences. The miniature uses a static taped bird and little behavioral change.
items.acceptance: The game makes the sequence and visible behavior clear enough to relate the boy's action to the words without asserting his unspoken motive as fact.

items.title: Tape, permission, and mending
items.current: There is no tape-fetch or repair interaction; the illustration starts with a tape-colored patch already present.
items.acceptance: Account for each intended event and object in the game world, with explicit control and consequence under Tony's world-gameplay rule.

items.title: Interpretation changes presentation meaningfully
items.current: Two picture buttons change a small illustration; the account and real adventure largely proceed identically.
items.acceptance: Make clear what this choice changes, why both supported interpretations are valid, and how the chosen emphasis appears in the eventual world contribution.

items.title: Consequences and misconception feedback
items.current: An optional text question and generic prepared help exist; live interpretation is unavailable.
items.acceptance: A misunderstanding about when the wing tore or why the boy hesitated receives evidence-based feedback without invented motives or a compulsory correct-answer gate.

items.title: Rehearsal and actual sharing stay separate
items.current: Records are separate internally, but reading from the backpack can expose picture choices and finishing the reader can record early sharing.
items.acceptance: The player knows whether they are inspecting, practising, choosing a picture, or actually sharing with Grandma or the gathering.

groups.title: Sol, the bakery, repair, and bread

items.title: Why Pip visits Sol
items.current: A goal points to the workshop, but the source page and ending choices dominate the first meeting.
items.acceptance: Establish Grandma's invitation, Sol's reluctance, his unfinished account, and the specific help he wants in a natural world encounter.

items.title: Sol's workshop and manuscript as usable objects
items.current: A façade, outside workbench, and page model exist. The child talks to Sol to open the page; tools have no gameplay role.
items.acceptance: Each intended workshop object has a clear purpose, available action, and visible response; scenery is not counted as interactive work.

items.title: Where and when the bakery story happens
items.current: Older written decisions treat it as Sol's earlier repair; Tony now explicitly requires the events to take place in the game. The premature flashback suggestion was rejected.
items.acceptance: Resolve this gap with Tony after the audit. No flashback, present-day retcon, controlled character, or additional mission is selected by this checklist.

items.title: Rina and her promised bread
items.current: Rina's request exists only in the manuscript. The player does not encounter her problem as an unfolding world situation.
items.acceptance: Establish Rina, what she promised, who depends on it, and why the flour and roof matter before asking about the ending.

items.title: Recognizable bakery
items.current: There is no playable bakery. A small building appears only inside an ending illustration.
items.acceptance: The required bakery events take place in the game with recognizable space, access, relevant objects, and a clear relationship to the current story.

items.title: Broken roof and incoming water
items.current: The illustration is built with the repaired roof/tile already in place. There is no damaged-to-repaired state or leak interaction.
items.acceptance: Show the actual fault, water entering, what is at risk, the repair action, and the stopped leak while outside rain remains distinct.

items.title: Flour sacks and the threat to them
items.current: Three static sacks decorate the illustration. No moving/protecting/checking sacks or changing condition exists.
items.acceptance: Flour condition and any intended player action affect or explain the consequence in the game, not only in the passage.

items.title: Wood, tools, and repair materials
items.current: There is no collection or use sequence. The older story specifies a cracked tile, so treating arbitrary wood as that repair would silently change the account.
items.acceptance: Account explicitly for Tony's requested material collection and the actual repair mechanism; provenance, ownership, use, and remaining material must be clear.

items.title: Player performs the intended repair
items.current: No command, world target, or state transition lets a player repair the bakery.
items.acceptance: The agreed repair interaction changes visible physical state and has a clear success/failure response and recovery path.

items.title: Observable repair consequence
items.current: The text states the flour stayed dry; the game does not show a before/action/after causal sequence.
items.acceptance: A child can observe why the repair changed what Rina could do and distinguish fixing the leak from changing the weather.

items.title: Bread being made
items.current: The illustration makes a completed loaf visible after 0.7 seconds. It has no visible flour-to-bread activity or baking sequence.
items.acceptance: Bread production follows the supported events with an understandable time transition and actual in-world activity; no invented crafting recipe is approved here.

items.title: Rina's thanks and the loaf
items.current: A tiny Rina model moves horizontally with a loaf in the rehearsal; no separate world visit or contextual handoff occurs.
items.acceptance: The child can see who thanks whom, why, where, and what the loaf represents in the actual story sequence.

items.title: Sol discovers why the small repair mattered
items.current: A writing prompt asks for the conclusion before the experience has established its cause and consequence.
items.acceptance: Sol's changed view follows the visible events and the child's contribution, making the ending a payoff to something that happened.

items.title: Consequence of an ineffective action
items.current: There is no bakery gameplay model, so there are no meaningful action outcomes or recoverable setbacks there.
items.acceptance: Define and show consequences for intended actions before calling this an interactive episode; the audit does not invent punishments or mandatory mistakes.

items.title: Sol prepares to participate
items.current: Choosing draft/ending changes flags and replies. The promised putting-away of the page and readiness movement are not clearly performed.
items.acceptance: Sol visibly retains the actual page, prepares it, and responds to the invitation; preparation, attendance, sharing, and stored story stay distinct.

groups.title: Writing, choosing, and performing Sol's ending

items.title: An ending to an established sequence
items.current: Finish the ending together jumps straight to original/later text, a writing prompt, and multiple control groups. Tony reasonably cannot tell what ending is being requested.
items.acceptance: The writer has just encountered the relevant situation, events, consequence, speaker, and purpose, and can identify what remains to be said.

items.title: Original account versus later information
items.current: Both headings exist, but FINISH_WITH_SOL discloses laterKnown and opens both immediately.
items.acceptance: Make clear which events were in Sol's draft, what he tells the child next, and how that supplies a possible ending.

items.title: One coherent writing interaction
items.current: Source, extra account, writing, word help, feedback, picture selection, try/use controls, and prepared endings coexist inside a dense reader.
items.acceptance: The child can follow one clear current activity and understand the next action without losing the source or mistaking tools for story choices.

items.title: Child's exact writing
items.current: Draft text, selected contribution, and revision are separate; later edits do not automatically replace the selected text.
items.acceptance: Preserve exact words through revision, reading practice, saving, selection, performance, and replay, with accurate authorship.

items.title: Meaning determines the performed scene
items.current: Try my ending directly uses the manually selected bread/thanks/both scene. Optional AI feedback may suggest a scene but is unavailable locally.
items.acceptance: The game truthfully relates the child's intended meaning to the supported world performance and asks for clarification when it cannot, without pretending a keyword or picture choice understood the writing.

items.title: Unsupported writing does not become Sol's fact
items.current: Any nonblank child contribution matching its revision can be selected and published as Sol's ending, even when it contradicts the source.
items.acceptance: Preserve the child's draft and a valid way forward while avoiding presenting unverified or contradicted writing as an event Sol witnessed; no AI score gate is required.

items.title: Try, revise, confirm, perform
items.current: Separate flags and controls exist, but rehearsal and results remain small pictures inside the learning area.
items.acceptance: The reading area handles wording and confirmation; the game world performs the corresponding scene and returns to the next meaningful interaction.

items.title: Prepared support and open draft
items.current: Prepared bread/thanks endings and a draft-discussion path exist; all can reach later states.
items.acceptance: They remain understandable supported alternatives with honest credit and equal story value, not buttons that conceal missing gameplay.

items.title: Selected ending changes the later contribution
items.current: Exact selected text and scene feed the gathering, but reactions and world performance are incomplete.
items.acceptance: The eventual sharing visibly uses what was actually prepared; subsequent edits or rehearsals cannot silently replace it.

items.current: The planner reduces time and speaker to adjacent button groups. It does not deliver the full agreed character-led sequence.
items.acceptance: Each decision follows what the player learned from that person and produces a comprehensible commitment in the world.

items.title: All three valid Mara arrangements
items.current: The three combinations are stored and used later; usual-time/Mara is rejected.
items.acceptance: Preserve all three and make their different attendance, teller/listener, timing, and reciprocal-sharing consequences observable.

items.title: Meaningful failed plan and revision
items.current: An unavailable combination shows a preview explanation and cannot be saved. Most other choices already work.
items.acceptance: The child can see why a plan fails a real constraint and how changing it alters what happens, consistent with agreed routes and without compulsory failure.

items.title: Actual in-person invitations
items.current: Distance checks and invitation state exist, but result replies frequently remain notices inside the same panel.
items.acceptance: The child sees who has heard which plan and the character's specific response before leaving to the next task.

items.title: Changing a plan already communicated
items.current: Old invitation expectations are retained until retold. The planner lists who needs an update.
items.acceptance: Ordinary play visibly carries the change through relevant people, with a clear reason to revisit and no unnecessary repeat trip.

items.title: Pip reports the arranged roles to Grandma
items.current: The planner reads global invitation flags. There is no distinct final player report of Mara's agreed role followed by Grandma's readiness exchange.
items.acceptance: Grandma receives the relevant arrangement through the agreed interaction; player/global knowledge cannot substitute for character communication.

items.title: Readiness is preparation, not a quiz
items.current: Before we begin lists state prerequisites. With many other actions present, it feels like a hidden task checklist.
items.acceptance: Each prerequisite was established as a natural story task; the child knows what remains and why without a clue count or answer score.

items.title: Story time advances at the event boundary
items.current: Begin gathering starts the arrival transition; reading duration does not advance story time.
items.acceptance: Make the time change clear in the game and preserve deliberate reading pace without a real-time penalty.

items.title: Passengers finish, then Mara travels
items.current: A short arrival animation exists for the later plan, but the preceding job context and work completion are weak.
items.acceptance: Show arrival, safe disembarkation, Mara finishing duty, and travel across the actual bridge in a readable sequence before she participates.

items.title: Sol's arrival with his chosen page
items.current: Sol walks from the workshop during arrival, with a page model. Preparation and the chosen version are mostly text.

groups.title: The gathering brings the threads together

items.title: An actual gathering in the game
items.current: Arrivals occur in the world, then the sequence becomes a stack of reading screens and next-story buttons; game characters mostly stand still.
items.acceptance: Confirmed actions return to a visible gathering with current speaker, listeners, page, response, and resulting story contribution.

items.title: Welcome reflects the chosen plan
items.current: Three correct welcome texts exist and practice is offered; its world performance is not connected to the child confirming the welcome.
items.acceptance: The appropriate speaker visibly welcomes the actual participants, with the correct reason for Mara's attendance or absence.

items.title: Mara's actual teller/listener role
items.current: Plan-dependent text says who is reading. The reader uses the same repair illustration and world speaker behavior is not clearly staged.
items.acceptance: Pip reading for absent Mara, Pip reading while she listens, and Mara telling are visibly different world events.

items.title: Prepared Sol ending and audience response
items.current: The selected ending is printed, then Invite/Next advances. The agreed bread-versus-thanks audience reaction is absent.
items.acceptance: Sol shares the chosen version and the audience responds specifically to the consequence or emphasis the child helped retain.

items.title: An open draft leads to real discussion
items.current: Two question buttons, replies, and add/keep choices exist inside the reader.
items.acceptance: The game's participants ask, answer, revise or retain the draft and respond visibly; no requirement to ask both questions or invent a finished ending.

items.title: Ending added during the gathering
items.current: ADD_ENDING changes state and prints the result, but a new in-world telling and audience response are not performed.
items.acceptance: Show the change as made during this discussion, then share the added ending without falsely claiming it was prepared earlier.

items.title: Grandma hears Sol's reason
items.current: The exact question and response are printed together in one screen.
items.acceptance: Show the actual exchange and Grandma's change of understanding as part of the gathering.

items.title: The Empty Bench explains the whole problem
items.current: The full story and chronology note exist; the world does not stage the earlier empty evenings and renewed welcome.
items.acceptance: Clearly connect her assumption to both actual reasons and her action now, while keeping earlier events distinct from the present.

items.title: Stories enter the garden as they are shared
items.current: NEXT_STORY flips record flags; NPC flowers appear without individual title/picture recording actions in the world.
items.acceptance: Each actual contribution changes its own existing lantern visibly and retains its author, text, selected image, and draft history.

items.title: All nine outcome combinations
items.current: Three Mara outcomes times three Sol outcomes are modeled and covered by prior contracts.
items.acceptance: Independently play the meaningful differences and see them reflected in world participants, contributions, closing duty, and narration; state combinations alone are insufficient.

items.title: Pip's lantern records a real event
items.current: Two choices change a miniature and a record flag; the world flower does not visibly display the chosen picture.
items.acceptance: The same planted flower gains the chosen actual planting or gathering moment, with correct participants and a clear meaning.

items.title: Mara attends and hears Grandma
items.current: Later-plan closing lines exist in the reader. The actual listening, acknowledgement, and departure context are weak.
items.acceptance: The world shows the reciprocal sharing the plan enabled, rather than just stating everyone had a chance.

items.title: Absent Mara receives a real copy
items.current: Copy and delivery actions have state and animation, but the reader can obscure the handoff.
items.acceptance: Grandma visibly gives the copy, Pip carries it across the retained bridge, and Mara receives it at work with an appropriate reply.

items.title: A conclusion to the original purpose
items.current: Finish the chapter is available after flags are satisfied, but the assembled screens have not made the renewal and contribution feel earned to Tony.

items.title: Return to Jo and ready Loop
items.current: The studio view returns and a reader contains four pictures. The whole-world presentation transition is weak.
items.acceptance: The game visibly returns to Jo/Loop and presents the ending produced by the adventure with clear optional watch/narrate choices.

items.title: Four pictures match actual events
items.current: Correct branch text and the selected Sol scene reach four miniature pictures. Their world presentation and correspondence to the child's written meaning remain unaccepted.
items.acceptance: Each picture and caption truthfully depicts the completed route, selected contribution, participants, and delivery or shared listening.

items.title: Pause and resume narration at a useful boundary
items.current: Only the picture number is stored. Watch restarts that paragraph, without the specified saved sentence position.
items.acceptance: Model listening and child-paced narration pause/resume without losing the current text or silently completing unread content.

items.title: Replay, explore, and start fresh
items.current: Pause/new-adventure archive and post-ending replay/explore controls exist; fresh start was inspected on the separate audit origin.
items.acceptance: Both cancellation and restart work without affecting other saves; replay does not duplicate game events, stories, or claimed learning.

items.title: Own reasoning versus supplied words
items.current: Typed explanations are saved, but later state changes do not use them. Report offers two buttons wired to the same event.
items.acceptance: Make clear when the child supplied reasoning, requested help, or asked Pip to explain; preserve the intended connection to the decision without claiming assessment.

items.title: Work-time inference
items.current: The later-time question exists, but the actual work conflict is not established visibly and live response interpretation is absent.
items.acceptance: The child's explanation can connect changed hours, final passengers, and gathering time using the relevant account and actual consequences.

items.title: Belief versus evidence
items.current: Grandma's letter and Mara's account can be compared in a details section. Correct reporting is supplied automatically.
items.acceptance: The player can distinguish Grandma's assumption from Mara's explanation, communicate relevant facts, and observe a changed response.

items.title: Cause, sequence, and a changed outcome
items.current: Sol's sequence is written, not played; questions ask for significance without the necessary experience.
items.acceptance: Connect leak, repair, dry flour, possible baking, and thanks through observable events and accurate language.

items.title: Plausible interpretation and uncertainty
items.current: The boy's motive is correctly treated as inference in provider instructions, but the usable demo cannot interpret a novel explanation.
items.acceptance: Discuss evidence and plausible uncertainty without forcing one private motive or rewarding keyword matching.

items.title: Consequences without an answer gate
items.current: Avoiding a compulsory correct answer has resulted in very few meaningful recoverable setbacks outside bridge construction.
items.acceptance: Preserve voluntary help and alternate valid outcomes while letting a mistaken plan or action produce a relevant, understandable world consequence.

items.title: No invented learning achievement
items.current: No child ability profile or mastery score is recorded. Technical tests and source exposure remain separate fields.
items.acceptance: Continue to distinguish participation, assistance, reading exposure, actual observed speech, comprehension evidence, and measured improvement.

items.acceptance: Provide a truthful, useful word-help path with exact occurrence/revision binding and a workable unavailable-service state.

items.title: Spelling suggestion, use, keep, undo

items.acceptance: The child explicitly chooses a valid suggestion for that occurrence or keeps their words, and can undo without unrelated text changes.

items.title: Disputing a wrong word explanation

items.acceptance: Model speech, recorded playback, microphone, word audio, route changes, and discarded attempts never overlap or leak into another activity.

groups.title: AI behavior, honesty, and implementation boundaries

items.title: Live understanding versus prepared help
items.current: The current authored demo returns unavailable for live text, word, transcription, and speech jobs. Prepared hints are not adaptive understanding.
items.acceptance: Demonstrate each promised AI job with honest provenance before presenting it as working. No provider call or activation is authorized by this audit.

items.title: Ambiguous or brief writing
items.current: Bounded status/feedback contracts exist, but actual semantic accuracy across short, unclear, paraphrased, or unusual answers is unqualified.
items.acceptance: Give specific clarification grounded in the text without replacing the child's answer or confusing brevity with lack of comprehension.

items.title: Feedback changes the right thing
items.current: Most feedback is optional text; a supported Sol result can only suggest a scene. Story progress still comes from separate commands.
items.acceptance: Explicitly identify what is adapted: explanation, hint, clarification, or supported scene suggestion, and what the child must confirm before world action.

items.title: Only disclosed sources and current revisions
items.current: Request IDs, revisions, source references, cancellation and strict server outputs exist; actual qualification remains open.
items.acceptance: Neither hidden later events nor stale answers can drive feedback or modify the current choice; world actions remain under the game coordinator.

items.title: User edits or disputes while waiting
items.current: Requests cancel on editing and one recheck is available; this is engineering scaffolding with synthetic coverage.
items.acceptance: Verify preserve/edit/stop/recheck/leave/retry sequences without stale replies, hidden retries, or lost writing.

items.title: Long draft span selection
items.current: Over 4,000 code points produces Choose a shorter part to discuss, but no actual span-selection control is provided.
items.acceptance: Keep the full draft and let the child explicitly select the shorter part for feedback rather than forcing deletion or silent truncation.

items.title: Truthful service availability and latency
items.current: Limits and unavailable states exist, but buttons often offer jobs whose unavailable status is explained only later.
items.acceptance: The demo clearly distinguishes usable local help from unavailable live feedback and remains playable during failure or slow response.

items.title: Qualification ledger and protected data
items.current: Provider qualification remains halted at 1/75; audio is temporary and keys are server-side.
items.acceptance: Preserve cap, records, no hidden requests, no child profile, and no persisted raw audio; resume only under the existing explicit coordinated authorization process.

items.current: Important world animations can run behind an open reader and most story performances happen inside miniature reader illustrations.
items.acceptance: Reading and confirmed choices lead back to visible world action and consequence, with a clear return point; apply this to every encounter.

items.title: One current task and next step
items.current: Goal card, notice, dialogue, action footer, library access, and workshop travel can compete; construction still showed the previous Talk to Mara suggestion.
items.acceptance: The child can identify the current task, available action, and reason for it in every mode and visit order.

items.title: Choices look like choices
items.current: Paired colored buttons and legends were added, but planner, source reading, support, continuation, and story actions still mix multiple groups.
items.acceptance: Identify whose choice is being made, what confirmation does, and which controls are reading help; color supplements clear text and state.

items.title: Every response identifies its speaker
items.current: Reply labels exist, but plain quoted greetings, notices, source paragraphs, and multiple simultaneous replies remain inconsistent.
items.acceptance: Every conversational turn is attributable and follows the child's actual choice in an understandable order.

items.title: Current passage remains usable
items.current: Large source, nested writing, feedback, and lower fixed actions produce competing scroll regions. In construction, key controls fall below the fold.
items.acceptance: Keep current text, relevant choice, and navigation usable at the demo viewport and larger text sizes without crowding the game or losing context.

items.title: Hints are discoverable and relevant
items.current: A prominent hint/status banner exists and fixes an earlier visibility complaint. Hints are mostly a single direct answer and can reflect generic rather than active subtask state.
items.acceptance: The child can find a small hint or fuller help, see what it refers to, and continue without an automatic solution or action.

items.title: Control meaning across modes
items.current: Movement, construction arrows, word navigation, text input, E, and Escape have guards, but their mode transitions and labels need coherent experience review.
items.acceptance: No held key crosses modes; an input always acts on the visible role/selection; confirm/cancel/back behave predictably.

items.title: Native equivalents for all world actions
items.current: Native bridge/movement controls exist. New required bakery/material/story-world actions have no corresponding controls because they are missing.
items.acceptance: Every implemented world action has usable keyboard and non-drag equivalents with clear focus and target feedback.

items.title: Continue returns to the right context
items.current: Many readers close to the garden globally, rather than restoring the immediate conversation or activity the child was doing.
items.acceptance: Returning from word help, source, story library, practice, draft and plan preserves the intended source/task and relevant position.

items.title: Visual and sensory access
items.current: Large text, roomier text, reduced motion, focus traps and some compact tests exist; full target-device, touch and screen-reader qualification is open.
items.acceptance: Demonstrate readable text/contrast, usable targets, focus return, sound-off play, reduced-motion consequences and appropriate compact layout without overstating device support.
